claims.text: Low-level carbon doping of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys enhances glass-forming ability.
Low-level carbon doping improves the thermal stability of the amorphous state in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys.
Arc-melted Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 can form an amorphous structure under rapid cooling without deliberate carbon addition.
A carbon-containing precursor or carbon-providing processing environment can introduce carbon into a forming compositionally complex alloy.
Melt spinning at cooling rates of 10^5–10^6 K/s can amorphize Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Pulsed laser ablation can provide kinetic control over amorphous phase formation in compositionally complex alloy nanoparticles.
Added carbon may be incorporated into the amorphous alloy matrix.
Added carbon may segregate into carbon-enriched surface layers.
Carbon-enriched surface layers act as diffusion barriers that hinder crystalline-phase nucleation and growth.
Carbon doping increases the effective configurational disorder of the alloy.
Carbon doping reduces atomic mobility and inhibits crystal nucleation.
Reduced atomic mobility and inhibited nucleation enhance glass formation and stabilize the amorphous phase during thermal exposure.
Carbon doping should increase the critical casting diameter or reduce the critical cooling rate required for amorphization relative to an undoped phosphorus-containing baseline.
Carbon doping should increase the onset crystallization temperature relative to an undoped phosphorus-containing baseline.
Carbon doping should reduce the DSC exothermic heat release relative to an undoped baseline.
Reduced DSC exothermic heat release indicates improved thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The beneficial effect should occur only when carbon is maintained at an optimized low concentration.
Excessive carbon may form carbides or secondary phases and compromise the amorphous state.
